A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Diffusion-EAGS, with matching authors, core procedures and substantial shared results despite the changed title. All 18 pages of v2 and 23 pages of v3, including appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original generation and translation experiments, component ablations, keyword-generation examples, and potential, entropy and diversity analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds human evaluations, GPT-4 preference judgments, dialogue summarization, and schedule and backbone comparisons.

M1.justification: EAGS, ENS and cross-entropy training are retained. The reported final selection changes from size-20 minimum Bayes risk decoding in v2 Sections 3.3/4.4 to generating 20 candidates and selecting five by perplexity in v3 Section 5.1/F.3. The D-cMRF formulation primarily changes the theoretical treatment.

E1.justification: v3 adds DialogSum dialogue summarization, a limited extension of the existing conditional-generation suite (Appendix F.2 and Table 10). Earlier tasks, including English–German translation, remain. OpenWebText disappears from the taxonomy table, but v2 does not establish its use in the work's experiments.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated LD4LG and GENIE comparisons on ParaDetox. Conversely, v2 Tables 12–14's GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 generator comparisons on Deontology, QQP and QG are removed. Their ParaDetox comparisons and the LLM diversity-saturation analysis remain; moving GPT-3.5 into the main tables is not itself a new baseline.

E3.justification: v3 introduces human MOS evaluation with four annotators, GPT-4 pairwise QG judging, reference-based ROUGE evaluation for DialogSum, and backbone and scheduling controls. It also reports PPL-based candidate selection instead of the earlier MBR description. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the newly disclosed test-set size does not establish a changed split.

E4.justification: v3 adds denoising-schedule experiments and failure examples, including uniform, reversed-entropy and EAGS selection (Appendix C), a BERT/RoBERTa/T5 comparison, and comparative ParaDetox output analysis (G.4/G.6). The original component ablation, keyword cases, entropy trajectories and diversity-saturation analysis are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports a ParaDetox PPL standard deviation of 61, human-rating standard deviations, and Fleiss' kappa above 0.7 (F.3/G.1/G.2). The earlier statement about sampling CDLM outputs with different seeds remains. No explicit increase in experimental runs is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds human scores, QG preferences, DialogSum results, LD4LG/GENIE scores and schedule/backbone outcomes. DialogSum ROUGE-1/2 is 0.409/0.174 for the proposed method. v2's ParaDetox PPL/MAUVE row of 69.5/0.773 reappears as BERT in v3 Table 15, while the main RoBERTa row becomes 109.3/0.811; because v2 named RoBERTa, this is revised attribution and reporting, not an established same-setting performance change. Several GPT-3.5/GPT-4 task-result rows are removed.

T1.justification: v3 replaces the earlier MRF exposition with an explicit energy-based D-cMRF formulation and adds an energy-reduction and convergence argument, including Equations 6–10 and Section 3.3.1's guarantees. v2 contains potential and conditional-probability derivations but no corresponding convergence argument.

C1.justification: v3 strengthens the central scientific contribution from empirically successful MLM/diffusion integration to a theoretically grounded process claimed to guarantee progressive energy reduction and stable convergence (Sections 1 and 3.3). The underlying claims of strong generation quality, diversity and token-level control remain.

C2.justification: v3 reinterprets the retained potential-shift experiment as motivating energy updates when conditioning changes. It adds explanations of T5's low diversity through initial decoder tokens and of competing models' termination and repetitive-generation problems, while qualifying transfer to other PLM architectures. The limitations add propagation of pretrained-model bias and remove the explicit entropy-computation-cost limitation.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies 20 held-out conditions with five outputs each, candidate-selection details, DialogSum's maximum length of 292, annotator qualifications and rating criteria, and the GPT-4 judge configuration. These improve documentation without establishing that existing sample counts changed. Core learning-rate, batch-size, hardware and translation settings remain.

R1.justification: v3 substantially reframes the work around autoregressive limitations, energy-based MLM interpretations and hybrid diffusion approaches. Newly cited work includes Goyal et al. (2022), Lin et al. (2023), Xiang et al. (2024) and Xu et al. (2025), alongside additional reasoning and diversity literature. This changes research positioning beyond the relocation of related work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before the method; task taxonomy, translation and diversity-saturation discussions move to appendices; algorithms are separated; and the conclusion gains a substantive discussion. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes.

P2.justification: v3 adds a motivation schematic and a quality–diversity scatterplot, substantially redraws the workflow figure, and splits the main ParaDetox presentation into quality and diversity tables with MOS. Existing plots and benchmark tables move to appendices, while new summarization, preference and backbone tables expand the displays. The scatterplot largely redisplays existing results.

improvement.justification: v3 adds valuable human validation, schedule/backbone controls and summarization evidence that v2 lacked. However, its new energy-reduction guarantee relies on an asserted inequality in Equation 8 rather than a derivation from the sampling rule. Its main quality MOS of 0.97 also conflicts with Appendix G.2's component means of 0.97 and 0.90, which imply 0.935 under F.3's averaging rule. Together with removed GPT comparisons on three tasks, these validity and reporting concerns prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
